messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Publishing with lavaan?
parts:
This sounds a bit like an "appeal to authority," a highly dubious debating tactic. I understand that if we were sending a spaceship full of colonists to Mars, we would want all calculations to be double-checked and triple-checked and as certain as they could possibly be. But it troubles me that we know so little about these numbers and rely upon them so blindly that we must fall back on such a defense. It is another dimension of uncertainty clouding the validity of our inferences.

On Sat, Mar 10, 2018 at 7:27 PM, Christopher David Desjardins <cddesj...@gmail.com> wrote:
Based on Google Scholar, it looks like Rosseel (2012) "lavaan: An R Package for Structural Equation Modeling" has been cited just under 3000 times. This is the citation that pops up when you type: citation("lavaan")

On Sat, Mar 10, 2018 at 6:15 PM, Christopher David Desjardins <cddesj...@gmail.com> wrote:
Yes, I have published multiple times using lavaan. Absolutely no one has ever requested that I use commercial software to replicate my results. Why should they? What makes you think the code and math are more correct in Mplus, Amos, etc? I have always been able to replicate methods papers with freely available data sets (e.g., papers by Curran, Muthen, Bollen, etc) with lavaan.

To some extent this email is a little insulting to Yves and all the folks that have worked so hard on lavaan, let alone the thousands of folks who have worked so hard to make R such an amazing platform for statistics, data visualization, machine learning, etc. Software that is both free and open-source. It's also a little dismissive to imply that lavaan is just for poor students. Commercial software is expensive even if you live in Europe or North America, is still a black box, and not always better ...

Would you write an email like this to the r-sig-mixed-models mailing list and ask them if they've ever published with lme4 or nlme?

I am guessing this email wasn't intended to be interpreted the way that I have. So, to answer your questions. I have published several times with lavaan, would definitely not tell a reviewer to use commercial software, and I do think your attitude is too conservative. In fact, I would applaud the authors for citing an R package because it's easy to forget.


On Sat, Mar 10, 2018 at 5:50 PM, Christopher Bratt <christop...@gmail.com> wrote:
I have switched back to using only Mplus, for the time being. One reason are hickups in lavaan that probably will be solved soon. But I also realised that it was not straight forward to reproduce in Mplus the model I had developed with lavaan for data with partly categorical indicators and cases with missing data. For some models, there may be some discrepancies in results, it seems. There are differences between commercial latent variable applications too, but these applications seem established and accepted by the community and journals.  

lavaan is still in its beta, so leaving students with a low budget aside, I would always make sure that for complex models, a commercial, established application will give similar results (pick one, they do not all use the same algorithms). Given my experiences, it seems better to develop everything from scratch in Mplus than trying to handle two applications for latent variables -- provided one has access to Mplus, that is. (I'm not so sure about Stata, for instance, I believe I would prefer lavaan.)

I think the lavaan project will become much bigger than it is now. But for the time being: does anyone publish using only lavaan? As a reviewer, I would request a comparison with more established software (in spite of the community control that is immanent in open source software). But is my attitude too conservative? Has lavaan become accepted for applied statistics in any mainstream journal?

--

messages.author: 572119bb37de95d7
messages.subject: Re: Publishing with lavaan?
parts:
Thanks, Ed. Well said.

I was glad to see you on this list, the man who -- among other things -- recommended Mplus to me many, many years ago (on SEMNET). 

I considered developing an analysis relying only on lavaan. Then I imagined a reviewer (or me as a reviewer)  seeing lavaan ast the program of choiice ("Lavaan is BETA software"). I  tend to do several different statistical analyses for one question, to be sure they converge on the same conclusion. But in this case the uncertainty was not about the correctness of conclusions derived from a single statistical approach. I was uncertain about the assumed legitimacy of the software itself, among scholars and reviewers. 

Your point applies to other applications too, and lavaan is not a black box like some other programs are. So, in the long run, our argument seems to be more in favour of lavaan than against it, I think. 

Glad to see you on the lavaan list!

Christopher
